questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Vertical Asymptotes of a Rational Function
questions.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
f(x)=\frac{x(x+3)}{(x+1)(x-4)}.
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)(x-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the two solutions $x=-1$ and $x=4.$ Therefore, the equations of the vertical asymptotes are $x=-1$ and $x=4.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-4}{{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{{x}^{2}(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)\cancel{(x+2)}}{{x}^{2}\cancel{(x+2)}} \\  & =\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}=0
$$

This gives the solution $x=0.$ Therefore, $x=0$ is the only vertical asymptote.

questions.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{5}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+x} \\  & =\frac{5}{x({x}^{2}+x+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives

$$
x({x}^{2}+x+1)=0.
$$

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

- Solving $2x=0$ gives the solution $x=0.$

- The equation ${x}^{2}+x+1=0$ has no real solutions because the discriminant $D$ is negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={1}^{2}-4(1)(1) \\  & =1-4 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only vertical asymptote is $x=0.$
